faq.a: No. FeNO assesses inflammation, while spirometry measures airflow limitation; both are complementary.
A high FeNO suggests eosinophilic bronchitis, which responds to inhaled steroids even without wheeze.
faq.q: Is FeNO useful in non‑asthma cough?

faq.a: Rely on clinical history, peak flow variability, and trial of inhaled steroids; reassess when the device is repaired.
faq.q: What if the FeNO analyser is broken?

exam: A 12‑year‑old with intermittent wheeze has a FeNO of 70 ppb but normal spirometry. What is the next step? — Start low‑dose inhaled corticosteroid and arrange follow‑up FeNO in 4 weeks.
A patient on high‑dose ICS still has FeNO 80 ppb and two exacerbations per month. Which therapy is indicated? — Consider adding an anti‑IL‑5 or anti‑IL‑4R biologic.
How does recent tobacco use affect FeNO interpretation? — It lowers FeNO, potentially masking eosinophilic inflammation; ask about smoking and interpret cautiously.

You have no FeNO device; a child presents with chronic cough and atopy. How do you decide on inhaled steroids? — Perform a therapeutic trial of inhaled steroids; improvement supports eosinophilic airway disease.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate referral for a patient with high FeNO? — Acute severe wheeze with hypoxia or rapid peak‑flow decline.

Differentiate FeNO from blood eosinophil count in asthma management. — FeNO reflects airway inflammation directly; blood eosinophils reflect systemic inflammation and may not correlate with airway disease.
Why might a patient with well‑controlled asthma still have FeNO >50 ppb? — Ongoing allergen exposure or suboptimal inhaler technique can maintain airway inflammation despite symptom control.
Explain how FeNO guides stepping down therapy. — If FeNO ≤25 ppb for ≥3 months, consider reducing inhaled steroid dose while monitoring symptoms.
ai.title: Exhaled Nitric Oxide in Asthma
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) reflects airway eosinophilic inflammation and helps diagnose and monitor asthma, especially in low‑resource settings where sputum eosinophils are unavailable.

b: Normal: ≤25 ppb in adults, ≤20 ppb in children
Elevated: >50 ppb strongly suggests eosinophilic asthma
sections.p: FeNO is the concentration of nitric oxide in a patient’s breath, measured in parts per billion (ppb). Elevated levels indicate eosinophilic airway inflammation, a hallmark of type‑2 asthma.

t.b: Does the patient have eosinophilic airway inflammation? – A result >50 ppb supports asthma; ≤25 ppb makes eosinophilic asthma unlikely.

b: Mild inflammation: 25–50 ppb
Moderate–severe: >50 ppb
sections.p: FeNO is not a severity score but correlates with inflammation intensity; higher values often accompany uncontrolled disease.

b: Allergic asthma (most common)
Atopic dermatitis with comorbid asthma
Eosinophilic bronchitis
Occupational exposures (e.g., wood dust)
Parasitic infections (e.g., helminths) can raise FeNO in some tropical settings
sections.p: Elevated FeNO occurs when type‑2 cytokines (IL‑4, IL‑13) up‑regulate inducible nitric oxide synthase in airway epithelium.

b: Variable symptoms, worse at night or after allergen exposure
May have normal spirometry early in disease
sections.p: Patients often have wheeze, cough, and dyspnoea that vary over time and with triggers. FeNO helps differentiate eosinophilic asthma from other causes of cough.

b: History of atopy, trigger exposure, medication use
Physical exam: wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase
sections.p: FeNO is part of a stepwise work‑up for chronic cough or suspected asthma, especially when sputum analysis is unavailable.

t.b: If peak flow meters are unavailable, rely on symptom diary.
Rule out alternative diagnoses (e.g., TB, pneumonia). – Normal film supports primary airway disease.

b: Repeated exacerbations requiring oral steroids
Progressive decline in FEV1 despite therapy
Acute severe wheeze with hypoxia
sections.p: Uncontrolled eosinophilic inflammation can lead to airway remodeling, frequent exacerbations, and respiratory failure.

b: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) – suppress eosinophilic inflammation; FeNO should fall >20 % after 2–4 weeks.
Add-on biologics (e.g., anti‑IL‑5, anti‑IL‑4R) for persistently high FeNO and severe disease.
Avoid oral corticosteroids unless an acute exacerbation occurs.
sections.p: Treat the underlying type‑2 inflammation first, then address symptoms and monitor with FeNO.

t.b: When FeNO device unavailable, use symptom control and spirometry trends.

b: Educate patients on trigger avoidance (dust, smoke, strong fragrances).
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce infection‑driven exacerbations.
sections.p: Regular FeNO checks (every 3–6 months) help tailor therapy and prevent exacerbations.

b: Blood eosinophils reflect systemic inflammation, not airway-specific inflammation.
Sputum eosinophils are gold‑standard but require lab facilities often lacking in low‑resource settings.
sections.p: FeNO is sometimes mistaken for blood eosinophil count or sputum eosinophils.

b: Recent smoking or exposure to NO‑producing pollutants lowers FeNO.
High dietary nitrate (e.g., leafy greens) can modestly raise FeNO.
Acute viral infection may suppress FeNO despite underlying eosinophilia.
sections.p: Certain factors can falsely lower or raise FeNO, leading to misinterpretation.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe wheeze with inability to speak full sentences
Rapidly falling peak flow (>30 % in 1 hour)
